claim: Prolonged exposure to loud noise causes damage to the stereocilia core of inner ear sensory hair cells.
source: Prolonged exposure to loud noise has been shown to affect inner ear sensory hair cells in a variety of deleterious manners, including damaging the stereocilia core.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by references to previous work showing damage visualized by TEM and confocal microscopy.

claim: Damaged sites in stereocilia cores can be visualized as 'gaps' in phalloidin staining of F-actin.
source: The damaged sites can be visualized as 'gaps' in phalloidin staining of F-actin
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 1.

claim: Monomeric actin, an actin nucleator, and crosslinker are enriched at gap sites, suggesting localized remodeling occurs to repair broken filaments.
source: the enrichment of monomeric actin at these sites, along with an actin nucleator and crosslinker, suggests that localized remodeling occurs to repair the broken filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous studies cited in the introduction.

claim: Gaps in mouse auditory hair cells are largely repaired within 1 week of traumatic noise exposure.
source: we show that gaps in mouse auditory hair cells are largely repaired within 1 week of traumatic noise exposure through the incorporation of newly synthesized actin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1E showing decrease in gap frequency over time.

claim: Newly synthesized actin is incorporated into stereocilia cores during gap repair.
source: we show that gaps in mouse auditory hair cells are largely repaired within 1 week of traumatic noise exposure through the incorporation of newly synthesized actin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 1K-L using EGFP-β-actin labeling.

claim: XIRP2 is required for the repair process of stereocilia F-actin gaps.
source: We provide evidence that Xin actin binding repeat containing 2 (XIRP2) is required for the repair process
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4 showing impaired repair in Xirp2 knockout mice.

claim: XIRP2 facilitates the enrichment of monomeric γ-actin at gaps.
source: We provide evidence that Xin actin binding repeat containing 2 (XIRP2) is required for the repair process and facilitates the enrichment of monomeric γ-actin at gaps.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 5 showing decreased γ-actin enrichment at gaps in Xirp2 knockout mice.

claim: Recruitment of XIRP2 to stereocilia gaps is force-dependent.
source: Recruitment of XIRP2 to stereocilia gaps and stress fiber strain sites in fibroblasts is force-dependent
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 7 using laser ablation experiments in fibroblasts.

claim: XIRP2 contains a novel mechanosensor domain located in its C-terminus.
source: Recruitment of XIRP2 to stereocilia gaps and stress fiber strain sites in fibroblasts is force-dependent, mediated by a novel mechanosensor domain located in the C-terminus of XIRP2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 7 showing CTD recruitment to stress fiber strain sites.

claim: Hair cells can recover from sublethal hair bundle damage.
source: Our study describes a novel process by which hair cells can recover from sublethal hair bundle damage
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the repair process described.

claim: The repair process may contribute to recovery from temporary hearing threshold shifts.
source: Our study describes a novel process by which hair cells can recover from sublethal hair bundle damage and which may contribute to recovery from temporary hearing threshold shifts
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 9 showing impaired recovery in Xirp2 knockout mice.

claim: The repair process may contribute to prevention of age-related hearing loss.
source: Our study describes a novel process by which hair cells can recover from sublethal hair bundle damage and which may contribute to recovery from temporary hearing threshold shifts and the prevention of age-related hearing loss.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 9 showing progressive hearing loss in Xirp2 knockout mice.

claim: The hair bundle is composed of F-actin-based stereocilia arranged in a staircase-like format.
source: The hair bundle, composed of filamentous (F)-actin-based stereocilia arranged in a staircase-like format, is deflected in response to mechanical stimulation
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about hair cell structure.

claim: Deflection of the hair bundle causes opening of mechanotransduction (MET) channels at stereocilia tips.
source: The hair bundle, composed of filamentous (F)-actin-based stereocilia arranged in a staircase-like format, is deflected in response to mechanical stimulation, which causes the opening of mechanotransduction (MET) channels at stereocilia tips (Hudspeth, 2005; Fettiplace, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Intense stimulation from loud noise can cause damage to stereocilia F-actin cores visible by TEM as disorganization of the paracrystalline structure.
source: Intense stimulation, such as from loud noise, can cause damage to the stereocilia F-actin cores, which is visible by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) as disorganization of the paracrystalline structure of negatively stained actin filaments (Tilney et al., 1982; Engström et al., 1983; Liberman, 1987; Liberman and Dodds, 1987)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to previous TEM studies.

claim: Damage to stereocilia cores is likely to decrease the rigidity of the bundle.
source: This damage is likely to decrease the rigidity of the bundle (Saunders et al., 1986a; Duncan and Saunders, 2000)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Decreased bundle rigidity could lead to reduced mechanotransduction.
source: This damage is likely to decrease the rigidity of the bundle (Saunders et al., 1986a; Duncan and Saunders, 2000), which could lead to reduced MET.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a logical inference from decreased rigidity.

claim: An active repair mechanism is needed to preserve hair cell function after stereocilia F-actin damage.
source: In order to preserve hair cell function, an active repair mechanism would be needed to repair any damage to stereocilia F-actin.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a logical necessity given the slow turnover of stereocilia actin.

claim: Passive repair through actin treadmilling is unlikely to be sufficient for stereocilia repair.
source: Passive repair through actin treadmilling is unlikely to be sufficient, because, unlike in most F-actin-based structures, F-actin turnover in stereocilia is mostly restricted to a dynamic zone at stereocilia tips (Zhang et al., 2012; Drummond et al., 2015; Narayanan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations about limited actin turnover in stereocilia.

claim: Monomeric β- and γ-actin are enriched at phalloidin-negative gaps in stereocilia F-actin.
source: Previous studies (Belyantseva et al., 2009; Andrade, 2015) found that monomeric β- and γ-actin, as well as the actin-associated factors cofilin and espin, are enriched at phalloidin-negative gaps in stereocilia F-actin.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction citing previous studies.

claim: Cofilin and espin are enriched at phalloidin-negative gaps in stereocilia F-actin.
source: Previous studies (Belyantseva et al., 2009; Andrade, 2015) found that monomeric β- and γ-actin, as well as the actin-associated factors cofilin and espin, are enriched at phalloidin-negative gaps in stereocilia F-actin.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction citing previous studies.

claim: Inner hair cell stereocilia in mice lacking γ-actin develop gaps in the absence of overstimulation.
source: It was also shown that inner hair cell (IHC) stereocilia in mice lacking γ-actin develop gaps in the absence of overstimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction citing previous work.

claim: γ-actin is likely important for the repair of gaps or in the prevention of their formation.
source: Therefore γ-actin is likely important for the repair of gaps or in the prevention of their formation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from the observation that γ-actin knockout mice develop gaps.

claim: Following 1 hr of 120 dB broadband noise, the percentage of IHCs with gaps increases from 3.76%±1.506 to 12.31%±3.369.
source: In adult mice, gaps are present in a small percentage of IHCs (3.76%±1.506) in mice unexposed to prolonged loud noise, but following 1 hr of 120 dB broadband (1–16 kHz) noise, this increases to 12.31%±3.369 (*, p=0.031) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results with specific quantitative data and statistical significance, and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Gap frequency increases from 4.89±1.97% to 21.39±4.29% one hour following 2 hr noise exposure.
source: Following an initial increase in gap frequency from 4.89±1.97% to 21.39±4.29% in mice 1 hr following noise (*, p=0.013)
evidence: This is stated in the results with specific quantitative data and statistical significance, and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Gap frequency decreases to 12.80±4.76% by 8 hr post noise.
source: the percent of IHCs with gaps decreased to 12.80±4.76% by 8 hr post noise (n.s., p=0.312)
evidence: This is stated in the results with specific quantitative data and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Gap frequency decreases to 4.00±1.76% by 1 week post noise.
source: and to 4.00±1.76% by 1 week post noise (**, p=0.008).
evidence: This is stated in the results with specific quantitative data and statistical significance, and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Gap frequency 1 week following noise exposure is not significantly different from baseline level.
source: Gap frequency 1 week following noise exposure was no longer significantly different from the baseline level (n.s., p=0.998)
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There is no significant increase in the number of dead IHCs at any time point after noise exposure.
source: There was no significant increase in the number of dead IHCs at any time point after noise (No Noise vs 1 hr, p=0.974, No Noise vs 8 hr, p=0.521, No Noise vs 1 week, p>0.999) (Figure 1F)
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: There is no significant change in IHC tallest row stereocilia number following noise exposure.
source: we also did not observe any significant change in IHC tallest row stereocilia number following noise exposure (No Noise vs 1 hr, p>0.999, No Noise vs 8 hr, p=0.969, No Noise vs 1 week, p=0.969) (Figure 1G)
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: EGFP-β-actin is localized only to stereocilia tips in FLEx-β-actin-EGFP mice when unexposed to noise.
source: Due to minimal actin turnover in stereocilia, when unexposed to noise, EGFP-β-actin is localized only to stereocilia tips in these mice as previously reported (Narayanan et al., 2015; Figure 1K–L, red arrows).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to previous work and shown in Figure 1K-L.

claim: Areas of enrichment of newly synthesized β-actin are observed in stereocilia following noise exposure, which are likely sites of repair.
source: Consistent with this, we see areas of enrichment of newly synthesized β-actin in stereocilia following noise exposure which are likely sites of repair (Figure 1K–L, yellow arrows).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1K-L with yellow arrows indicating enrichment sites.

claim: XIRP2 immunostaining is enriched at gaps in noise-induced IHC stereocilia.
source: In addition to these, we observe the enrichment of XIRP2 immunostaining at gaps (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: XIRP2 immunostaining is enriched at naturally occurring gaps in vestibular hair cells of the utricle.
source: This enrichment is observed in both naturally occurring gaps in murine auditory IHCs of the cochlea (Figure 2A) and vestibular hair cells of the utricle (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: XIRP2 shows an approximately 1.4-fold increase in intensity in the center of a phalloidin-negative gap compared to the surrounding area.
source: A representative line scan plotting the fluorescence of XIRP2 shows an approximately 1.4-fold increase in XIRP2 intensity in the center of a phalloidin-negative gap compared to the surrounding area of the stereocilia core (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results with quantitative data and shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: In larger phalloidin-negative gaps, XIRP2 enrichment is sometimes observed only at the gap edges.
source: Occasionally, in larger phalloidin-negative gaps, we observe a gap in the XIRP2 staining as well, with enrichment only at the gap edges (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: XIRP2 enrichment is present in gaps induced by loud noise exposure.
source: XIRP2 enrichment is present both in gaps induced by loud noise exposure (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: XIRP2 enrichment is present in gaps occurring in Ptprq knockout mice.
source: and in gaps occurring in genetic models of hair bundle degeneration (Goodyear et al., 2012; Krey et al., 2018), including Ptprq (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: XIRP2 enrichment is present in gaps occurring in Elmod1 knockout mice.
source: and Elmod1 knockout mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: XIRP2 enrichment is present at gaps in human utricle hair cells.
source: Additionally, we confirmed that this staining pattern is present in human utricle hair cells, as well (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: XIRP2 is no longer enriched at gaps in Xirp2 knockout mice.
source: To ensure that the enrichment of XIRP2 immunostaining at these sites was not an artifact of antibody staining, we found that XIRP2 was no longer enriched at gaps in Xirp2 knockout mice (Francis et al., 2015; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3F, confirming antibody specificity.

claim: Short XIRP2 isoform is enriched at gaps.
source: Moreover, we see XIRP2 enrichment at gaps using a second XIRP2 antibody specific for the short isoform, which is localized to the hair bundle (Figure 3G)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Long XIRP2 isoform is not enriched at gaps.
source: but not an antibody specific for the long isoform, which is primarily localized to other F-actin-based hair cell structures (Francis et al., 2015; Figure 3H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3H.

claim: XIRP2 appears to remain enriched at repaired gaps.
source: Interestingly, XIRP2 appears to remain enriched at repaired gaps, as we see colocalization of XIRP2 enrichment at sites labeled by enriched β-actin synthesized after noise exposure (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The number of XIRP2-enriched sites in stereocilia cores does not significantly decrease 1 week following noise exposure.
source: Consistent with this, we also see an enrichment of XIRP2-enriched sites in stereocilia cores, which does not significantly decrease 1 week following noise exposure (No Noise vs 1 hr, *, p=0.0391; 1 hr vs 8 hr, n.s., p=0.956; 8 hr vs 1 week, n.s., p=0.989; No Noise vs 1 week, n.s., p=0.227) (Figure 3J)
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3J.

claim: At P20, 14.88±1.96% of utricle hair cells in Xirp2 knockout mice have gaps compared to only 4.54±0.70% in wild-type mice.
source: At P20, 14.88±1.96% of utricle hair cells Xirp2 knockout mice had gaps compared to only 4.54±0.70% of cells in wild-type (WT) mice (***, p=0.001) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with specific quantitative data and statistical significance, and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There are significantly more IHCs with gaps in P20 Xirp2 knockout mice compared to wild-type.
source: At the same age, there were also significantly more IHCs with gaps in Xirp2 knockout mice compared to WT (**, p=0.002) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical significance and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Gaps may build up over time in the absence of XIRP2.
source: These results, concordant with a previous report of F-actin filament disorganization in a different Xirp2-null mouse line (Scheffer et al., 2015), suggest that gaps may build up over time in the absence of XIRP2.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the increased gap frequency in Xirp2 knockout mice.

claim: In wild-type mice, the percent of cells with gaps is no longer significant from baseline levels by 1 week after noise.
source: In WT mice, after an initial increase 1 hr post noise (***, p<0.001), the percent of cells with gaps was no longer significant from baseline levels by 1 week after noise (n.s., p=0.950).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In Xirp2 knockout mice, the percent of cells with gaps further increases during the week following noise exposure.
source: However, in Xirp2 knockout mice, although we observed a smaller, non-significant (p=0.617) initial increase in cells with gaps after noise, the percent of cells with gaps actually further increased from baseline levels during the following week (*, p=0.0140) (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Gaps are not efficiently repaired in the absence of XIRP2.
source: rather than decreasing to pre-noise levels like in WT, suggesting that gaps are not efficiently repaired in the absence of XIRP2.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the gap frequency data in Xirp2 knockout mice.

claim: γ-actin immunostaining is enriched in gaps in hair cell stereocilia.
source: As was previously shown (Belyantseva et al., 2009), γ-actin immunostaining is enriched in gaps in hair cell stereocilia.
evidence: This is stated in the results citing previous work.

claim: γ-actin at gap sites is likely to be primarily monomeric.
source: γ-Actin at these sites is likely to be primarily monomeric, as the phalloidin signal is weak, and DNaseI staining, which labels monomeric β- and γ-actin (Mannherz et al., 1975), is also enriched at phalloidin-negative gaps (Belyantseva et al., 2009; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting evidence from DNaseI staining and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: γ-actin shows an ~2.7-fold increase at the center of phalloidin-negative gaps compared to the surrounding region.
source: A representative plot of the fluorescence intensity of γ-actin staining in a utricle hair cell (Figure 5B and C) shows an ~2.7-fold increase at the center of the phalloidin-negative gap compared to the surrounding region.
evidence: This is stated in the results with quantitative data and shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: γ-actin no longer appears to be enriched in gaps in Xirp2 knockouts.
source: However, in contrast to WT mice, γ-actin no longer appears to be enriched in gaps in Xirp2 knockouts (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: The ratio of γ-actin fluorescence intensity at the center of phalloidin-negative gaps compared to the edge decreases from 2.03±0.16-fold in WT utricles to 1.29±0.06-fold in Xirp2 knockout utricles.
source: On average, the ratio of γ-actin fluorescence intensity at the center of phalloidin-negative gaps compared to the edge of gaps decreases from 2.03±0.16-fold in WT utricles to 1.29±0.06-fold in the absence of XIRP2 (***, p=0.0008) (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is stated in the results with specific quantitative data and statistical significance, and shown in Figure 5J.

claim: There is a decrease in the enrichment of γ-actin in noise-induced gaps in Xirp2 knockout IHCs.
source: We also found a decrease in the enrichment of γ-actin in noise-induced gaps in Xirp2 knockout IHCs (**, p=0.0048) (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical significance and shown in Figure 5K.

claim: β-actin enrichment in gaps decreases from 1.440±0.080-fold in WT to 1.144±0.0314-fold in Xirp2 knockout mice.
source: Although smaller than for γ-actin, we additionally observe a decrease in enrichment of β-actin in gaps from 1.440±0.080-fold in WT (Figure 5F and L) to 1.144±0.0314-fold in Xirp2 knockout mice (**, p=0.0098) (Figure 5G and L).
evidence: This is stated in the results with specific quantitative data and statistical significance, and shown in Figure 5F-G and L.

claim: Espin enrichment in gaps is decreased in Xirp2 knockouts.
source: Similarly, espin enrichment in gaps is also decreased in Xirp2 knockouts (***, p=0.0003) (Figure 5H, I, M).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical significance and shown in Figure 5H-I and M.

claim: The sensory hair bundle harbors the short XIRP2 isoform.
source: We reported previously that the sensory hair bundle harbors the short XIRP2 isoform, which is distinguished from the canonical long isoform by the lack of the Xin repeats encoded by exon 7, and by the presence of a LIM domain and a CTD that are encoded by exon 8 and exon 9, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results citing previous work by the authors.

claim: A 1 bp substitution in exon 8 (T1187A) introduces a stop codon before the beginning of the LIM domain in short XIRP2 without altering the amino acid coding sequence of the long isoform.
source: However, by making a 1 bp substitution in exon 8 (T1187A, KM273012.1), we were able to introduce a stop codon before the beginning of the LIM domain in short XIRP2 (L396*, AIR76303.1) without altering the amino acid coding sequence of the long isoform (V3255V, NP_001077388.1) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the genetic engineering approach and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Truncated short XIRP2 (XIRP2-ΔLIM/CTD) does not undergo nonsense-mediated decay, but is still expressed and localizes to the hair bundle.
source: Truncated short XIRP2 (XIRP2-ΔLIM/CTD) does not undergo nonsense-mediated decay, but is still expressed and localizes to the hair bundle, as XIRP2 staining with an antibody recognizing the N-terminus of both isoforms is still present in stereocilia (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Long XIRP2 is still primarily localized to the cuticular plate and cell junctions in Xirp2ΔLIM/CTD mice.
source: Confirming that the bundle staining in the Xirp2ΔLIM/CTD mice was not due to compensatory relocalization of long XIRP2, we found that long XIRP2, recognized by an antibody against the alternative reading frame in exon 8, is still primarily localized to the cuticular plate and cell junctions (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: XIRP2-ΔLIM/CTD shows less enrichment in phalloidin-negative gaps.
source: Despite XIRP2-ΔLIM/CTD's colocalization with stereocilia actin cores, accordant with our hypothesis, XIRP2-ΔLIM/CTD shows less enrichment in phalloidin-negative gaps (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The enrichment of XIRP2 fluorescence intensity at the center of gaps decreases from 1.27±0.02-fold in WT mice to 0.85±0.03-fold in Xirp2ΔLIM/CTD mice.
source: The enrichment of XIRP2 fluorescence intensity at the center of gaps decreases from 1.27±0.02-fold in WT mice to 0.85±0.03-fold in Xirp2ΔLIM/CTD mice (***, p<0.0.0001) (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is stated in the results with specific quantitative data and statistical significance, and shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The average ratio of γ-actin enrichment is decreased to 1.34±0.09-fold in the Xirp2ΔLIM/CTD mice.
source: The average ratio of γ-actin enrichment is decreased to 1.34±0.09-fold in the Xirp2ΔLIM/CTD mice (***, p<0.001) and is not significantly different from the 1.286±0.057-fold enrichment in WT mice (n.s., p=0.975) (Figure 6J)
evidence: This is stated in the results with specific quantitative data and statistical significance, and shown in Figure 6J.

claim: XIRP2 gap enrichment is necessary for subsequent recruitment of γ-actin.
source: indicating that XIRP2 gap enrichment is necessary for subsequent recruitment of γ-actin.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the γ-actin enrichment data in Xirp2ΔLIM/CTD mice.

claim: There is an increase in the percentage of utricle hair cells with gaps in Xirp2ΔLIM/CTD mice compared to WT.
source: In line with this, we found an increase in the percentage of utricle hair cells (Figure 6K) and IHCs (Figure 6L) with gaps compared to WT (*, p=0.0255 and **, p=0.007, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical significance and shown in Figure 6K-L.

claim: Xirp2ΔLIM/CTD mice exhibit a mild but significant increase in hearing thresholds compared to WT mice.
source: Albeit not as severe as the phenotype in Xirp2 knockout mice, Xirp2ΔLIM/CTD mice exhibit a mild but significant increase in hearing thresholds compared to WT mice, as measured by ABR (*, p=0.031) (Figure 6M)
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical significance and shown in Figure 6M.

claim: Gap repair may be important for maintaining hearing sensitivity.
source: suggesting that gap repair may be important for maintaining hearing sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the hearing threshold data in Xirp2ΔLIM/CTD mice.

claim: Expression of full-length XIRP2 partially labeled the actin cytoskeleton in fibroblasts.
source: Expression of full-length XIRP2 partially labeled the actin cytoskeleton (Figure 7C)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The single LIM domain of XIRP2 was cytoplasmic in fibroblasts.
source: while the single LIM domain of XIRP2 was cytoplasmic (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Neither full-length XIRP2 nor the single LIM domain were recruited to the induced strain site in stress fibers.
source: Neither full-length XIRP2 (Figure 7C–E) nor the single LIM domain (Figure 7F–H), however, were recruited to the induced strain site in the stress fiber (Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7C-H and Videos 1-2.

claim: The isolated CTD displayed a mild localization to the actin cytoskeleton in the basal state.
source: Unexpectedly, however, the isolated CTD displayed a mild localization to the actin cytoskeleton in the basal state (Figure 7I)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The isolated CTD showed strong recruitment to the ablation site in stress fibers.
source: and strong recruitment to the ablation site (Figure 7I–K; Video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7I-K and Video 3.

claim: Mechanosensitivity in XIRP2 is regulated, potentially via autoinhibition by the N-terminal domain.
source: The mechanosensitivity of the CTD, but lack of such behavior in the full-length XIRP2 protein, suggests that mechanosensitivity in XIRP2 is regulated, potentially via autoinhibition by the N-terminal domain (NTD).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the differential behavior of CTD vs full-length XIRP2.

claim: The 470 amino acid long sequence of XIRP2's CTD contains a novel mechanosensor domain.
source: Together these findings establish that the 470 amino acid (aa) long sequence of XIRP2's CTD contains a novel mechanosensor domain
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the mechanosensitivity experiments.

claim: Both endogenous γ- and β-actin are co-immunoprecipitated with EGFP-tagged short XIRP2 in NIH-3T3 cells.
source: Both endogenous γ- and β-actin are co-immunoprecipitated in NIH-3T3 cells transfected with EGFP-tagged short XIRP2, evidence for a direct or indirect binding (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: EGFP-XIRP2 pulls down both WT and G13R mutant γ-actin.
source: When NIH-3T3 cells were co-transfected with EGFP-tagged short XIRP2 and HA-tagged γ-actin or a polymerization-incompetent γ-actin mutant (G13R) (Posern et al., 2002), both WT and mutant γ-actin were co-immunoprecipitated (Figure 8B)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: XIRP2 has the capacity to bind to monomeric actin.
source: suggesting that XIRP2 has the capacity to bind to monomeric actin.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the co-immunoprecipitation with G13R mutant actin.

claim: Both full-length XIRP2 and the CTD were able to co-immunoprecipitate HA-tagged γ-actin (G13R).
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, both full-length XIRP2 and the CTD were able to co-immunoprecipitate HA-tagged γ-actin (G13R) (Figure 8C)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The CTD is sufficient to bind to monomeric actin.
source: suggesting that the CTD is sufficient to bind to monomeric actin.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Full length XIRP2 and the NTD displayed a high degree of colocalization with phalloidin in NIH-3T3 cells.
source: Full length and the NTD displayed a high degree of colocalization with phalloidin, and minimal localization in the cytosol.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The CTD of XIRP2 was predominantly localized in the cytosol, with occasional localization at a subset of stress fibers.
source: The CTD, in contrast, was predominantly localized in the cytosol, with occasional localization at a subset of stress fibers (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 8D (note: text says 8C but likely refers to 8D).

claim: XIRP2 binds to F-actin, presumably through its NTD.
source: Taken together, XIRP2 binds, either directly or indirectly, to F-actin, presumably through its NTD
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the colocalization and co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: XIRP2's interaction with monomeric actin is likely mediated by its CTD.
source: while its interaction with monomeric actin is likely mediated by its CTD.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: The CTD is expected to contain a mechanosensor domain as well as a monomeric actin binding domain.
source: The CTD is thus expected to contain a mechanosensor domain as well as a monomeric actin binding domain.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the mechanosensitivity and binding data.

claim: Xirp2 knockout mice on C57Bl/6J background develop high-frequency hearing loss by 7–8 weeks of age.
source: We previously reported that Xirp2 knockout mice, which were maintained on a C57Bl/6J background, develop high-frequency hearing loss by 7–8 weeks of age (Francis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results citing previous work by the authors.

claim: By 11 weeks, the hearing loss in Xirp2 knockout mice worsens to affect all frequencies.
source: Here, we expanded those studies and show that by 11 weeks, the hearing loss worsens to affect all frequencies (Figure 9A) (***, p<0.001)
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical significance and shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Hearing loss in Xirp2 knockout mice progressively worsens over time, as observed at 20 and 40 weeks.
source: and progressively worsens over time, as observed at 20 (Figure 9B) (***, p<0.001) and 40 weeks (Figure 9C) (***, p<0.001).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical significance and shown in Figure 9B-C.

claim: ABR thresholds in CBA/J Xirp2 knockout mice are not significantly elevated at 11–12 weeks of age.
source: Although the hearing loss is less severe in CBA/J Xirp2 knockout mice, and ABR thresholds are not significantly elevated at 11–12 weeks of age (Figure 9D) (n.s., p=0.090)
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 9D.

claim: CBA/J Xirp2 knockout mice develop a mild hearing loss at all frequencies by 20 weeks.
source: CBA/J Xirp2 knockout mice develop a mild hearing loss at all frequencies by 20 weeks (Figure 9E) (***, p<0.001)
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical significance and shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Hearing loss in CBA/J Xirp2 knockout mice further progresses by 40 weeks.
source: which further progresses by 40 weeks (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Following noise exposure, Xirp2 knockout mice displayed a smaller temporary threshold shift compared to WT.
source: Following the noise exposure, we surprisingly saw a smaller TTS in the Xirp2 knockout mice compared to WT, as indicated by lower hearing thresholds 1 day following noise (**, p=0.007) (Figure 9H).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical significance and shown in Figure 9H.

claim: 2 weeks following noise exposure, Xirp2 knockout mice displayed a larger permanent threshold shift than WT.
source: However, 2 weeks following the noise exposure, the Xirp2 knockout mice displayed a larger PTS than WT, with higher hearing thresholds across all measured frequencies at this time point (**, p=0.009) (Figure 9I).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical significance and shown in Figure 9I.

claim: There is a decrease in recovery during the 2-week period following noise exposure in Xirp2 knockout mice.
source: For each individual mouse, we measured the change in threshold between 1 day and 2 weeks following noise exposure and found a decrease in recovery during this period in Xirp2 knockout mice (Figure 9J) (**, p=0.005)
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical significance and shown in Figure 9J.

claim: Gap repair contributes to recovery from noise-induced hearing loss.
source: in accordance with our hypothesis that gap repair contributes to recovery from noise-induced hearing loss.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the hearing recovery data in Xirp2 knockout mice.

claim: Hair cells must withstand continuous mechanical stress despite being built to be delicate and fragile.
source: The long-term maintenance of sensory hair cells faces a fundamental challenge: to maximize sensitivity, hair cells are built to be delicate and fragile, yet they have to withstand continuous mechanical stress.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a general principle about hair cell biology.

claim: A potent capacity for repair must be considered indispensable for mammalian auditory hair cells that are not regenerated.
source: A potent capacity for repair must therefore be considered indispensable, especially for mammalian auditory hair cells that are not regenerated.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a logical conclusion from the lack of hair cell regeneration in mammals.

claim: XIRP2 senses stereocilia F-actin lesions in a force-dependent manner.
source: In our study, we provide evidence for a novel process that repairs lesions in the stereocilia F-actin core. We showed that the hair cell protein XIRP2, mediated by its mechanosensitive CTD, senses stereocilia F-actin lesions in a force-dependent manner
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the main findings.

claim: XIRP2 organizes the repair of F-actin lesions through F-actin remodeling.
source: and subsequently organizes the repair of the lesion through F-actin remodeling.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the main findings.

claim: Gaps in phalloidin staining likely represent areas with decreased actin filament density.
source: These changes in actin visualization likely represent areas with decreased actin filament density, where actin filaments have been broken and depolymerized due to mechanical forces from overstimulation or changes in stereocilia ion concentrations from increased MET
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of what gaps represent.

claim: Phalloidin binds at the interface of actin monomers within filaments.
source: as phalloidin binds at the interface of actin monomers within filaments (Barden et al., 1987; Cooper, 1987).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Gaps in the F-actin core are expected to decrease the structural integrity of the hair bundle and lead to impaired MET.
source: Even in the absence of other hair bundle damage that occurs in concert with the stereocilia breakage during noise exposure (Wagner and Shin, 2019), we expect that gaps in the F-actin core decrease the structural integrity of the hair bundle and lead to impaired MET.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a logical inference.

claim: In vitro fluid jet overstimulation of the hair bundle causes a decrease in bundle stiffness without breakage of interstereociliary links.
source: Previous work has shown that in vitro fluid jet overstimulation of the hair bundle causes a decrease in bundle stiffness (Saunders et al., 1986a; Saunders et al., 1986b; Duncan and Saunders, 2000) without breakage of interstereociliary links (including the tip links)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion citing previous work.

claim: Recovery of bundle stiffness was observed and is dependent on hair cell metabolic activity.
source: Consistent with our observed repair of stereocilia cores through actin remodeling, recovery of bundle stiffness was observed (Saunders et al., 1986a; Duncan and Saunders, 2000), dependent on hair cell metabolic activity (Saunders et al., 1986a).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion citing previous work.

claim: Stereocilia actin is stable, except for a small dynamic region at the very tips.
source: In contrast, stereocilia actin is stable, except for a small dynamic region at the very tips (Zhang et al., 2012; Drummond et al., 2015; Narayanan et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion citing previous work.

claim: The stable nature of stereocilia actin prevents damaged regions from being replaced passively through turnover.
source: preventing the damaged region from being replaced passively through turnover and necessitating an active repair mechanism to restore bundle rigidity and MET function.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a logical inference from the stable nature of stereocilia actin.

claim: Short filaments spanning the length of the gap are synthesized and attached to existing undamaged regions of the actin core through direct annealing.
source: As we did not observe EGFP-labeled β-actin along the whole length of the stereocilia following noise, we propose that short filaments spanning the length of the gap are synthesized and attached to existing undamaged regions of the actin core through direct annealing, which has been described in vitro (Murphy et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposed mechanism for repair.

claim: The decrease in monomeric actin gap localization is potentially the primary reason for the lack of gap repair in Xirp2 knockout mice.
source: The decrease in monomeric actin gap localization is potentially the primary reason for the lack of gap repair that we observe in Xirp2 knockout mice
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Short XIRP2 specifically and exclusively localizes to the hair bundle.
source: We previously reported that among the multiple XIRP2 isoforms expressed in hair cells, short XIRP2 (Genbank ID KM273012) specifically and exclusively localizes to the hair bundle (Francis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion citing previous work by the authors.

claim: The LIM domain and CTD of short XIRP2 are important for targeting XIRP2 to F-actin lesion sites.
source: Our studies on the Xirp2ΔLIM/CTD mice, where the LIM domain and CTD of the short isoform are removed, demonstrated the importance of these domains for targeting XIRP2 to the F-actin lesion sites.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the Xirp2ΔLIM/CTD mouse data.

claim: A subset of LIM domain proteins is unique in that their affinity to F-actin is 'switched on' by binding to strained F-actin.
source: A subset of LIM domain proteins, however, is unique in that their affinity to F-actin is 'switched on' by binding to strained F-actin (Sun et al., 2020; Winkelman et al., 2020; Sala and Oakes, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion citing recent work on mechanosensitive LIM domain proteins.

claim: LIM domain proteins have been shown to recruit repair proteins to strain sites.
source: These proteins have been previously shown to recruit repair proteins to these strain sites (Uemura et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion citing previous work.

claim: The first LIM domain from the protein testin was shown to recognize strained F-actin on its own.
source: While previous studies have suggested that strain recognition requires multiple LIM domains in series (Sun et al., 2020; Winkelman et al., 2020), the first LIM domain from the protein testin was recently shown to recognize strained F-actin on its own (Sala and Oakes, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion citing recent work.

claim: It is the isolated CTD of XIRP2 that is sufficient for recruitment to stress fiber strain sites.
source: Surprisingly, however, it was the isolated CTD of XIRP2 that we found was sufficient for recruitment to these strain sites.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the mechanosensitivity findings.

claim: Mechanosensitivity is not found in the full-length XIRP2 protein, suggesting that XIRP2's mechanosensitivity is regulated.
source: Interestingly, mechanosensitivity is not found in the full-length XIRP2 protein, suggesting that XIRP2's mechanosensitivity is regulated, potentially in an autoinhibitory manner, reminiscent of the reported behavior of testin (Sala and Oakes, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The CTD of XIRP2 constitutes a novel class of mechanosensitive protein domain.
source: It is our leading hypothesis that the CTD of XIRP2 constitutes a novel class of mechanosensitive protein domain.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as the authors' hypothesis.

claim: The CTD helps recruit additional repair factors including monomeric actin and the crosslinker espin to gaps.
source: The CTD also helps recruit additional repair factors including monomeric actin and the crosslinker espin to gaps
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: XIRP2 functions not only as a damage sensor, but also as an organizer of the subsequent actin remodeling efforts.
source: suggesting that XIRP2 functions not only as a damage sensor, but also as an organizer of the subsequent actin remodeling efforts.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: High frequency and amplitude deflection of hair bundles may induce localized stress along the shafts of stereocilia.
source: Nonetheless, it is plausible that high frequency and amplitude deflection of hair bundles induces localized stress along the shafts of stereocilia, causing focal destabilization and depolymerization of actin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a plausible mechanism.

claim: XIRP2 may have a further role following the repair of the actin core, possibly in reinforcing the structure at vulnerable sites.
source: However, if this is not the case, it may indicate that XIRP2 has a further role following the repair of the actin core, possibly in reenforcing the structure at vulnerable sites.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculation about XIRP2's continued presence at repaired sites.

claim: The build-up of unrepaired gaps in the Xirp2ΔLIM/CTD mouse likely leads to the development of hearing loss.
source: If, as we suspect, XIRP2-ΔLIM/CTD is still able to perform the other functions of XIRP2, the build-up of unrepaired gaps in the Xirp2ΔLIM/CTD mouse likely leads to the development of hearing loss in these mice, even in the absence of noise trauma.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the hearing loss in Xirp2ΔLIM/CTD mice.

claim: The role of XIRP2 in undamaged regions of the stereocilia core may also play an important role in the maintenance of hearing function.
source: However, the mild hearing phenotypes suggest that the role of XIRP2 in undamaged regions of the stereocilia core may also play an important role in the maintenance of hearing function.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the mild phenotype.

claim: The build-up of unrepaired gaps in the absence of XIRP2 may lead to progressive hearing loss.
source: The build-up of unrepaired gaps in the absence of XIRP2 may lead to the worsening phenotype, suggesting that gap repair could be necessary for the prevention of age-related hearing loss.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the progressive hearing loss data.

claim: Gap repair could be necessary for the prevention of age-related hearing loss.
source: suggesting that gap repair could be necessary for the prevention of age-related hearing loss.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the progressive hearing loss data.

claim: The phenotype in Xirp2 knockout mice is exacerbated when backcrossed to the C57Bl/6J strain, which harbors a mutation in CDH23.
source: Interestingly, the phenotype seems to be exacerbated when the Xirp2 mutation was backcrossed to the C57Bl/6J strain, which harbors a mutation in the tip-link protein, CDH23.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an observation from the data.

claim: Weakened or non-functional tip links may make hair cells more sensitive to the development of gaps.
source: An intriguing possibility is that weakened or non-functional tip links make hair cells more sensitive to the development of gaps and intensify the effect of the loss of XIRP2.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculation about the interaction between Cdh23 and Xirp2 mutations.

claim: Repair of tip links has been hypothesized to contribute to the decrease in hearing thresholds following an initial large temporary threshold shift.
source: Repair of other hair bundle structures like tip links (Zhao et al., 1996; Indzhykulian et al., 2013), which are broken following noise exposure (Pickles et al., 1987; Husbands et al., 1999), has been hypothesized to contribute to the decrease in hearing thresholds following an initial large TTS.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion citing previous work.

claim: The increased susceptibility of Xirp2 knockout mice to permanent noise-induced hearing loss is consistent with actin core repair contributing to threshold recovery.
source: The increased susceptibility of Xirp2 knockout mice to permanent noise-induced hearing loss is consistent with actin core repair also contributing to this threshold recovery.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the noise-induced hearing loss data.

claim: Repair of gaps is only one of many factors contributing to recovery from noise-induced hearing loss.
source: The relatively small difference between genotypes was unsurprising, however, if repair of gaps is only one of many factors contributing to this recovery, most of which we do not predict to be altered in the absence of XIRP2.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the modest effect size.

claim: There is evidence to suggest that unrepaired damage to the hair bundle plays a role in the development of noise-induced hearing loss.
source: However, there is evidence to suggest that unrepaired damage to the hair bundle, possibly including actin core lesions, also plays a role in the development of noise-induced hearing loss (Liberman and Dodds, 1987).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion citing previous work.

claim: Hearing performance in humans might better correlate with hair bundle morphology than hair cell numbers.
source: More recently, a human cadaver analysis from the Liberman lab concluded that hearing performance in humans might better correlate with hair bundle morphology than hair cell numbers (Wu and Liberman, 2022)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion citing recent work.

claim: Hair cells might persist with damaged hair bundles in a hypo-functional state.
source: This study also implied that hair cells might persist with damaged hair bundles in a hypo-functional state, opening up a treatment window for strategies to boost hair bundle repair and function.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion citing recent work.

claim: Repair mechanisms are necessary to restore MET and prevent hearing loss due to the inability of mature mammalian hair cells to regenerate.
source: This study sheds further light on the importance of repair of sublethal damage to hair cells in order to preserve hearing function following traumatic noise exposure and in aging animals. Due to the inability of mature mammalian hair cells to regenerate (Groves, 2010; Burns and Corwin, 2013), repair mechanisms are necessary to restore MET and prevent hearing loss.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion with supporting citations.

claim: Stereocilia actin cores are capable of recovery in mammalian hair cells.
source: Herein, we add stereocilia actin cores to the growing list of hair cell structures, including tip links (Indzhykulian et al., 2013), and controversially, synapses (Kujawa and Liberman, 2009; Shi et al., 2013), capable of recovery in mammalian hair cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study.
